figures.description: Vane Shear Test Applies when measuring undrained shear strength and sensitivity of soft to stiff clays and silts using the in situ vane shear test. VST measures undrained shear strength (su,fv), remolded shear strength (sur,fv), and sensitivity (St,fv) using maximum and residual torque. figures.description: Wedge Failure Applies when evaluating factor of safety against wedge failure for a rock slope with two intersecting discontinuity planes. Wedge failure involves two intersecting release planes (Plane A = flatter, Plane B = steeper) forming a sliding wedge. Geometric requirement: ΨFi > Ψi > φ′, where ΨFi is slope face inclination perpendicular to the line of intersection and Ψi is the dip of that line. ΨFi differs from ΨF unless the line of intersection dip direction matches the slope face dip direction. Basic analysis assumes friction only on Plane A and Plane B; normal forces RA and RB are computed from wedge weight components. Wedge factor K relates FW to equivalent plane failure factor of safety; K is determined graphically. Cohesion and water pressure require more detailed analysis;

figures.caption: Rock Slope Subject to Toppling Failure
figures.description: Toppling Failure Applies when assessing the risk of toppling failure for rock columns with steeply dipping, thin-bedded discontinuities at a slope face. Toppling occurs when the center of gravity of a rock column is on the slope-face side, creating eccentric loading. Eccentric loading generates tensile stress on the back face of the column; failure occurs when tensile capacity is exceeded. Toppling analyses are substantially more complex than plane or block failure analyses. Hand calculation methods from FHWA (1998) exist but have limited applicability to real field conditions.

Natural water content-based correlations for Cc show better mutual agreement than liquid limit or void ratio-based correlations. General form: Mds = α · qc, with α ranging 0.4 to 8; most soils fall between α = 1 and 3. α values compiled by Mitchell and Gardner (1975) vary with soil type and cone geometry — check applicability before use. Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) provide a normalized CPTu-based chart correlation for clays using corrected tip resistance qt (Figure 8-47).

figures.caption: Correlation between Modified Secondary Compression Index and Natural Water Content for Normally Consolidated Clays (after Mesri 1973, Holtz and Kovacs 1981)
figures.description: Coefficient of Secondary Compression Applies when estimating secondary (creep) compression settlement after primary consolidation is complete, particularly for NC clays, organic soils, and peats. Cεα = 0.0001 · wn (Eq. 8-35) estimates modified secondary compression coefficient from natural water content for NC clays. For most OC clays, Cεα ranges from 0.0005 to 0.001 (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990). figures.description: Correlations with Undrained Shear Strength Applies when estimating undrained Young's modulus for fine-grained soils using known undrained shear strength, PI, and OCR. Eu/su ratio is a function of plasticity index (PI) and overconsolidation ratio (OCR) per Duncan and Buchignani (1987). Correlation is based on direct simple shear test results. figures.description: Correlations with Standard Penetration and Pressuremeter Tests Applies when estimating undrained Young's modulus of clays from pressuremeter or SPT N values. PMT directly measures horizontal soil modulus; in clays this is approximately equal to undrained Young's modulus (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990). Ohya et al. (1982) correlation relates EPMT to SPT N value for clays (Figure 8-52). Correlation has high scatter (r² = 0.39) and should be used with caution. SPT-based estimates of Eu for clays are inherently uncertain due to scatter.

figures.caption: Undrained Modulus for Deep Foundations in Compression (after Poulos and Davis 1980)
figures.description: Correlations to Load Tests Applies when estimating undrained Young's modulus for clays supporting deep foundations or spread foundations using load test data. Poulos and Davis (1980) relate Eu to undrained shear strength for drilled shafts and driven piles in compression (Figure 8-53). Callanan and Kulhawy (1985) provide Eu correlations for drilled shafts (compression and uplift) and spread foundations (uplift) (Figure 8-54). For spread foundations, Eu is normalized by the mean total vertical stress (σvm) over foundation depth. Load test back-calculations offer site-specific modulus estimates that may be more reliable than index correlations.

figures.caption: Correlations for Drained Young's Modulus of Granular Soils
figures.description: Correlations with SPT N Values Applies when estimating drained Young's modulus for coarse-grained soils (sands, silts with sand, gravels with sand) using SPT N values. Multiple correlations exist for drained E of coarse-grained soils from SPT N; all normalize E by atmospheric pressure (Pa). Ferrent (1963): E ≈ 7.1(1−ν²)·N·Pa for sandy soils. Webb (1969): E ≈ 4.7(N+15)·Pa for sands; E ≈ 3.1(N+5)·Pa for clayey sands. Begemann (1974): E ≈ C(N+6)·Pa for N<15; E ≈ C(N+6)−39.5·Pa for N≥15, with C depending on soil type. Kulhawy and Mayne (1990): E ≈ 5·N60·Pa (sands with fines), 10·N60·Pa (NC clean sands), 15·N60·Pa (OC clean sands). N60 (energy-corrected blow count) should be used for modern samplers per Kulhawy and Mayne (1990).

figures.caption: Range of CBR based on DCP Predicted by Correlations
figures.description: Correlations with Dynamic Cone Penetration Applies when estimating CBR from Dynamic Cone Penetration (DCP) test results in the field or laboratory, particularly for pavement subgrade evaluation. The general DCP-CBR relationship is a power law: CBR = A·DCP^x, where A and x are empirically determined coefficients (Eq. 8-37). Coefficients A and x vary widely by researcher and soil type; A ranges from 25 to 501 and x ranges from -0.55 to -2.00 (Table 8-24). Nazzal (2003) provides a nonlinear alternative (Eq. 8-38) valid for DCP values of 6.3–67 mm/blow. Figure 8-56 illustrates the scatter in predicted CBR across multiple DCP correlations, highlighting uncertainty in selection. Some correlations are soil-type specific (e.g., fine-grained, coarse-grained, CL with CBR < 10).

Figure 8-57 presents the original data supporting this correlation. This correlation enables CBR estimation directly from routine SPT data without additional testing.
